summary: Defines two SDP attributes, group and mid, which group several media lines in a session description for purposes such as lip synchronization or receiving one flow in several formats on different ports. It was replaced by RFC 5888.

plainLanguage.summary: A video call has a sound track and a picture track. This tags them so they can be grouped and played in step with each other.

subtitle: Tags for linking audio, video, and related media streams in session descriptions.

tldr.problem: Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions with multiple media streams (audio, video, etc.), but provides no way to express relationships between them, such as which streams should be played in synchronization.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two SDP attributes: 'mid' (media stream identification) to tag each media line with a unique identifier, and 'group' to explicitly group media lines by relationship type (lip synchronization or flow identification).
tldr.outcome: Applications can now coordinate multiple media streams in a single session and handle scenarios like different codecs on different ports. The mechanism was later updated in RFC 5888.

facts.label: Attribute scope
facts.value: mid is media-level; group is session-level

today: RFC 5888 supersedes RFC 3388 with improved semantics and syntax for media line grouping. RFC 3388 is now Historic but remains the original definition of the problem and solution.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SDP session descriptions typically contain multiple media lines (called 'm' lines), each representing a separate media stream such as audio, video, or a shared whiteboard. When a session description contains more than one media line, SDP provides no standard way to express relationships between them. Applications receiving such descriptions must guess what the relationship is, or use out-of-band information.

This RFC extends SDP with two new attributes to allow the expression of how different media streams within a session description relate to each other: the 'mid' (media stream identification) attribute to label each media line, and the 'group' attribute to indicate groups and their relationship type.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a video call invitation, you list the audio track and video track separately. These tags help the receiver know they belong together and how they should be treated.

sections.title: The Mid and Group Attributes
sections.content:
The mid attribute provides a unique identifier for each media line within a session description. Each media line that participates in grouping must have a mid attribute with a unique identification tag. The identification tag is a simple token.

The group attribute is a session-level attribute that lists identification tags to group together media lines. The group attribute specifies the semantics of the grouping through a semantics field. All 'm' lines of a session that uses 'group' MUST be identified with a 'mid' attribute, whether they appear in the group line or not. If any media line lacks a mid identifier, the application MUST NOT perform any grouping.
sections.plainLanguage: The mid tag is like a sticker on each track that says 'I'm the audio' or 'I'm the video'. The group tag lists which stickers go together and why.

sections.title: Lip Synchronization (LS)
sections.content:
The first grouping semantics defined by the RFC is LS (Lip Synchronization). When media lines are grouped with LS semantics, the application MUST synchronize the playout of the corresponding media streams. This ensures that audio and video, for example, play at the same time so that the speaker's lips match the audio.

For RTP streams, synchronization typically uses RTCP, which provides enough information to map timestamps from different streams into wall-clock time. However, LS semantics can also apply to non-RTP media streams, in which case the application must use whatever mechanism is available to recover the original timing relationship between the streams.
sections.plainLanguage: If two tracks are in the same group with LS, they play together at the same speed. If the audio says 'hello' while the lips show 'goodbye', something is wrong.

sections.title: Flow Identification (FID)
sections.content:
The second grouping semantics is FID (Flow Identification). FID handles scenarios where a single media instance (for example, one audio stream) is sent using multiple RTP sessions. A typical example is cellular systems using different ports for different audio codecs, or systems where DTMF tones are received on a different host than the voice data.

When using FID semantics, a media agent sends a copy of the encoded media to each media line in the flow, as long as the codec in that line matches the currently active codec and the direction attribute permits sending. At any given moment, only one codec is active, so media is sent to different addresses depending on which codec is in use. Multiple media lines in an FID group may share the same codec; in this case, media is sent to all matching destinations simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the same audio stream needs to be sent to two different destinations because they support different types of encoding. FID says 'send it to both places, matching whatever format each can handle'.

sections.title: Usage in SIP
sections.content:
SDP descriptions are used by several protocols; SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) is the primary user. The RFC includes guidance on how grouping attributes should be used when SDP is carried in SIP offer/answer exchanges. The 'mid' value in an offer MUST be the same as the 'mid' value in the answer, and subsequent offers (such as re-INVITES) SHOULD use the same 'mid' value for existing media streams.

SIP entities that receive offers with group attributes they do not understand MUST ignore the group attribute but still include the mid attributes in their answer. If a media stream changes its mid identifier between offer and answer, the application must ignore all mid and group lines. For backward compatibility, systems that do not support these attributes simply ignore them.
sections.plainLanguage: When two phones exchange plans about which audio and video tracks to use, they need to agree on the same tags. If one phone says 'audio is mid:1' and the other says 'audio is mid:2', they ignore the grouping.

sections.title: Status and Relation to RFC 5888
sections.content:
RFC 3388 was a Proposed Standard published in December 2002. It defined the foundational mechanism for grouping media lines in SDP. The framework proved useful, but was later refined and updated by RFC 5888, which provides a cleaner syntax and better definitions of the grouping semantics.

RFC 3388 is now Historic, having been superseded by RFC 5888. Applications should prefer RFC 5888 for new implementations, but RFC 3388 describes the original design and remains relevant for understanding the history and rationale behind media line grouping in SDP.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC was the first to solve the problem, but a newer RFC (5888) does the job better. It is still accurate, but newer systems use the updated version.
